patient.chief_complaint: Increasing confusion and lethargy over three days
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. G. is a 59-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 15) and known moderate ascites who was brought to the emergency department by his daughter for three days of worsening confusion and progressive lethargy. His daughter reported that he had been increasingly difficult to rouse from sleep, was disoriented and repeating himself, and had stopped eating over the prior 48 hours. He had no witnessed vomiting, no hematemesis, no dark stools, and no gross change in urine output. She denied any recent alcohol consumption but was not fully certain, as the patient lived with her and had prior episodes of covert drinking. He had been compliant with his lactulose per his daughter's report. On presentation he was lethargic, disoriented to time and place, and unable to give a reliable history. He denied headache, neck stiffness, or photophobia. His daughter denied any focal limb weakness, facial droop, or new falls. He had no prior episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy. Notably, he was afebrile on arrival and his white blood cell count was within normal limits, reassuring at first glance. His abdomen was moderately distended with ascites and he had mild diffuse tenderness on palpation but no peritoneal signs. No source of infection was initially apparent. Chest radiograph was clear.

output.query: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis diagnosis management hepatic encephalopathy precipitant

results.title: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines — Management of ascites, SBP and hepatorenal syndrome in cirrhosis (2010)
results.summary: SBP is diagnosed by an ascitic fluid PMN count >=250 cells/mm3, regardless of culture result (culture-negative SBP represents approximately one-third of episodes). First-line treatment is intravenous cefotaxime or a third-generation cephalosporin. Albumin infusion (1.5 g/kg on day 1, 1 g/kg on day 3) reduces the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome and improves survival in patients with elevated bilirubin or creatinine.

results.title: AASLD 2014 HE Practice Guideline — Precipitant identification and management
results.summary: Infection, particularly spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, is a major precipitant of hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis. All patients with cirrhosis and ascites who present with encephalopathy should undergo diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP, even in the absence of fever or leukocytosis. The inflammatory response in cirrhosis is often blunted, and normal WBC does not exclude infection.

output.proposed: Cefotaxime (or ceftriaxone) for SBP plus lactulose continuation; review for CNS depressants and hepatic dose adjustments
interactions: Cefotaxime/ceftriaxone — no significant interaction with spironolactone, furosemide, lactulose, propranolol, or allopurinol
Spironolactone and furosemide — combination increases hyponatremia risk in cirrhotic patients already hyponatremic (Na 130); renal function and electrolytes should be monitored closely
Propranolol — beta-blockade may blunt the tachycardic response to infection; hemodynamic monitoring recommended during SBP treatment
Allopurinol — renally cleared; dose reduction if creatinine rises
contraindications: Benzodiazepines — contraindicated in hepatic encephalopathy; precipitate and prolong encephalopathy
Sedating opioids — avoid in hepatic encephalopathy; impaired hepatic metabolism prolongs effect and worsens encephalopathy
warnings: Lactulose — continue at current dose, titrate to 2-4 soft stools/day; monitor for hypernatremia if aggressive titration in setting of poor oral intake
Rifaximin — non-absorbable; minimal systemic drug interaction risk; compatible with current regimen
Empiric IV thiamine before any dextrose-containing fluids in patients with chronic alcohol use history
output.formulary_status: Cefotaxime and ceftriaxone on formulary. Rifaximin on formulary.
alternatives: Ofloxacin (oral) for SBP in patients without recent quinolone exposure and without vomiting, renal failure, or encephalopathy — less suitable here given encephalopathy grade
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily as equivalent alternative to cefotaxime

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 15), precipitated by spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

differential.diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy without identified infection (multifactorial — hyponatremia, poor intake, cirrhosis decompensation)
differential.key_features: Elevated ammonia, asterixis, cirrhosis — HE pattern is present regardless; SBP is the critical precipitant to identify, not exclude the HE diagnosis.
Abstinence reported by family but unverifiable; serum ethanol undetectable; no tremor, autonomic instability, or hyperreflexia to suggest withdrawal syndrome.
INR 2.0 and platelets 94 raise hemorrhagic risk; non-contrast CT head excludes acute intracranial blood.
Na 130 mEq/L — mild hyponatremia that can contribute to confusion but does not fully account for grade II HE or the severity of the ascitic cell count.
Chronic alcohol use history present; no ophthalmoplegia or nystagmus on exam; MRI periaqueductal/mammillary signal not sought but thiamine should be given empirically.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, lactate, coagulation. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for infection and metabolic precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Cirrhosis features (albumin 2.3, INR 2.0, bilirubin 4.2); ammonia 112 µmol/L; WBC 6.8 (normal — blunted inflammatory response); mild hyponatremia Na 130; ethanol undetectable.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, mass, large infarct) before further workup.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No acute intracranial abnormality; mild cortical atrophy; no hemorrhage, mass, or mass effect.

optimal_actions.action: Diagnostic paracentesis — send ascitic fluid for cell count with differential (PMN count), protein, SAAG, Gram stain, culture (inoculate blood culture bottles at bedside). Mandatory in any cirrhotic with ascites presenting with encephalopathy, regardless of fever or WBC.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ascitic PMN 412 cells/mm3 — exceeds the diagnostic threshold of 250 cells/mm3, consistent with neutrocytic ascites (SBP). Culture growing gram-negative rod.

optimal_actions.action: Literature/guideline search to confirm SBP diagnostic threshold, management protocol (antibiotic choice, albumin infusion), and the relationship between SBP and HE precipitants in cirrhosis.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD 2014 and EASL 2010 guidelines retrieved confirming PMN >= 250 cells/mm3 as diagnostic; normal WBC does not exclude SBP in cirrhosis; albumin infusion reduces hepatorenal syndrome risk.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review — evaluate empiric antibiotic choice (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone) against current regimen; confirm no CNS-depressant medications; review propranolol in context of infection-related hemodynamic instability; flag benzodiazepine and opioid risks.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No major interaction between cephalosporin and current regimen; propranolol may blunt fever/tachycardia response; benzodiazepines and sedating opioids contraindicated in HE.

optimal_actions.action: Consult hepatology for coordinated management of SBP-precipitated HE, albumin infusion protocol, rifaximin initiation, renal function monitoring for hepatorenal syndrome, and transplant candidacy assessment.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology confirms SBP-precipitated HE; initiates cefotaxime + albumin; titrates lactulose; adds rifaximin; plans 48-hour repeat paracentesis.

optimal_actions.action: Draw two sets of blood cultures, aerobic and anaerobic, before the first antimicrobial dose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Growth identifies the organism and its susceptibility; a negative or pending culture does not exclude the diagnosis, and yield falls once treatment has started

optimal_actions.action: Perform a diagnostic paracentesis and send ascitic fluid for cell count with differential, protein and culture, inoculating blood-culture bottles at the bedside
optimal_actions.expected_finding: A polymorphonuclear count at or above 250 cells/mm3 establishes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is a precipitant that must be treated whether or not fever or leucocytosis is present

optimal_actions.action: Send urine for microscopy and culture as part of the infection screen
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Pyuria and bacteriuria identify a urinary source; a negative result removes it from the list of precipitants

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis warranting echocardiography in this presentation.
Amyloid PET has no role in workup of acute metabolic encephalopathy; reversible HE precipitated by SBP is the diagnosis under evaluation.
Alzheimer genetic panel has no role in HE workup; acute metabolic encephalopathy in a cirrhotic is the clinical question.

harmful_tools.rationale: Lumbar puncture is not indicated — there is no clinical suspicion for meningitis (no neck stiffness, no photophobia, no fever, no focal signs). Performing LP without this indication, particularly in a coagulopathic patient (INR 2.0, platelets 94), risks procedural hemorrhage without diagnostic benefit.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect and hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk, especially in a coagulopathic cirrhotic.

critical_actions: Perform diagnostic paracentesis in any cirrhotic with ascites presenting with altered mental status — regardless of fever or peripheral WBC — to exclude SBP.
Initiate empiric third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime 2 g IV every 8 hours, or ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily) once ascitic PMN >= 250 cells/mm3 confirmed; do not await culture results.
Administer IV albumin (1.5 g/kg on day 1, 1 g/kg on day 3) to reduce hepatorenal syndrome risk in SBP with elevated bilirubin or creatinine.
Initiate lactulose titrated to 2-4 soft stools/day and add rifaximin 550 mg BID to treat HE.
Administer empiric IV thiamine before any dextrose-containing fluids given chronic alcohol use history.
Monitor renal function (creatinine, urine output) daily — SBP is a major trigger of hepatorenal syndrome in cirrhosis.
Repeat diagnostic paracentesis at 48 hours to confirm PMN response to treatment.
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute altered mental status to HE alone without performing diagnostic paracentesis — SBP must be excluded in every cirrhotic with ascites and encephalopathy.
Do not be reassured by normal WBC and absence of fever — the systemic inflammatory response is frequently blunted in cirrhosis; SBP can present without fever or leukocytosis.
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for agitation or alcohol withdrawal in this patient — they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy.
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — impaired hepatic metabolism prolongs effect and worsens encephalopathy.
Do not perform lumbar puncture in this patient — no clinical indication for LP, and coagulopathy (INR 2.0, platelets 94) increases procedural hemorrhage risk.
key_reasoning_points: SBP commonly presents without fever and without peripheral leukocytosis in cirrhotic patients — up to 30% of episodes are afebrile and WBC may be normal or low (hypersplenism); the blunted inflammatory response is well-recognized but clinically dangerous if used to incorrectly exclude infection.

The diagnostic criterion for SBP is ascitic fluid PMN >= 250 cells/mm3, independent of culture result, fever, or peripheral WBC — culture-negative SBP (approximately one-third of episodes) is treated identically to culture-positive SBP once the PMN threshold is met.

Every cirrhotic with ascites presenting with altered mental status requires diagnostic paracentesis as part of the standard workup — infection is a major and potentially reversible precipitant of HE, and missing it is a significant safety event.

Ammonia elevation supports the HE diagnosis but does not identify the precipitant — an elevated ammonia in a cirrhotic with AMS and ascites does not close the workup; paracentesis must still be performed.

Albumin infusion alongside antibiotic therapy for SBP reduces the incidence of hepatorenal syndrome (type 1 AKI) and improves 90-day survival in patients meeting criteria; this is a time-sensitive intervention.
Propranolol may mask the tachycardic response to infection (blunting fever and HR rise), further contributing to the clinically subtle presentation of SBP in this patient.

red_herrings.data_point: WBC 6.8 x10^9/L (within normal limits) and temperature 37.1°C (afebrile)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reassure the agent that infection is absent and attribute AMS to HE alone without performing paracentesis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Normal WBC and absence of fever do not exclude SBP in cirrhosis — the inflammatory response is frequently blunted by hypersplenism, immunosuppression from liver failure, and beta-blockade. Paracentesis is mandatory regardless of peripheral leukocyte count or temperature.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Treat elevated ammonia as sufficient explanation for AMS and close the precipitant workup without proceeding to paracentesis.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Elevated ammonia confirms hyperammonemia consistent with HE but does not identify the precipitant. The precipitant workup is mandatory; infection (SBP especially) must be excluded. Ammonia level alone is not a substitute for paracentesis in a cirrhotic with ascites and AMS.
